abstract: This paper examines why misinformation persists in society and why it continues to influence people's reasoning even after it has been corrected or retracted. Using the example of the false belief linking childhood vaccinations to autism, the authors review the psychological mechanisms behind the acceptance, persistence, and continued influence of misinformation. They discuss why corrections often fail and offer evidence-based recommendations for reducing the impact of false information.
key_claims: Misinformation is widespread and persistent in contemporary societies, with real-world consequences such as reduced vaccination rates and increased vaccine-preventable disease.
Corrections and retractions frequently fail to eliminate the influence of misinformation, a phenomenon known as the continued influence effect.
The persistence of misinformation stems from identifiable cognitive and social mechanisms rather than mere ignorance.
Debiasing is possible but requires strategies informed by psychological research.
methods: Interdisciplinary review and synthesis of psychological and cognitive science literature on misinformation, memory, and belief updating.
Analysis of real-world case examples, notably the discredited vaccine-autism link, to illustrate mechanisms and consequences.
findings: Retracted misinformation continues to shape beliefs and inferences even when people acknowledge and remember the correction (continued influence effect).
Factors including source credibility, repetition, fluency, and consistency with prior beliefs affect whether misinformation is accepted and retained.
Simply retracting or negating false information can be ineffective and may sometimes reinforce it.
Effective corrections tend to provide alternative causal explanations, warn about potential misinformation, and avoid repeated exposure to the myth.
contributions: Provides an integrative framework explaining the cognitive origins and persistence of misinformation.
Translates psychological research into practical, evidence-based recommendations for correcting misinformation and debiasing beliefs.
Bridges academic psychology with public policy and communication concerns around public health and misinformation.
framing: The paper sits within cognitive and social psychology, drawing on research on memory, belief updating, and reasoning to address the applied problem of misinformation in public discourse and public health communication.
